utterances.text: What was the political aim of the SDS party in relation to Dubrovnik? Can you say? The main theme.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: In the close vicinity of Dubrovnik lies the town of Trebinje which is where the SDS party was very strong. And some people from Dubrovnik did have links with that party. However, in Dubrovnik itself, Dubrovnik proper, there were some members who, shall we say, were malicious with respect to Croatia at that time. But the president of the SDS himself in Dubrovnik, who was elected then, was, according to my assessment, a very normal man. He wasn't malicious at all, the president himself, as opposed to some others whom I couldn't qualify in that same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say they were malicious with respect to Croatia, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, look at it this way: At that point in time, people started thinking about, or rather, you felt the mood change; democracy had arrived, was coming, and Croatia quite certainly would no longer be in the same position that it had been up until then. And quite normally, some people on the Croatian side were very enthusiastic about this fact and showed it. On the other hand, we saw the advent of their - when I say "their," I mean the Serb side - their line of thinking that they wouldn't serve the new authorities and that the police began -- when the uniforms of the police force took on Croatian insignia and emblems, those who belonged to the Serb people in Dubrovnik and were in the police force - and there were quite a large number of them - they didn't want to accept that. This led to outbreaks of various kinds. There were songs that were sung, provocations made, and the hopes were expressed that nothing would happen of that expected Croatia. And that was the prevalent mood during those times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the Serbs discriminated in Dubrovnik? Were they, for instance --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they dismissed from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No. There were dismissals in the police force, people were dismissed from their jobs, and the reason for that was that some people did not want to accept the insignia and emblems that I mentioned a moment ago. As to other dismissals from jobs, I don't know about those. Perhaps somebody was dismissed, but because he had made a misdemeanour or offence on the job, but not because they were Serbs, not because a person was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Serbs continue to hold positions in the government of -- in the town government or the public institutions, before the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Despite this, did the media in Serbia and Montenegro describe the situation of the Serbs in Dubrovnik as endangered? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. And very intensively, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were there reports about the destruction of Serb homes in Dubrovnik? And if so, what was the -- what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were reports of that kind, too. I remember a particular heading, a title - I don't remember the newspapers it appeared in, whether it was the Politika or Politika Ekspres newspaper, I don't remember now - but the heading was "Poljanic --" that is to say myself -- "Destroys 400 Serb Homes in Dubrovnik." I didn't destroy a single home. But what it was all about was that when we arrived in 1990, when we came into power in Dubrovnik, we inherited the fact that in the Dubrovnik municipality, it's an unbelievable number, but there are about 7.000 houses that were built without building permission. Among these 7.000 houses and facilities that were built, some of them already had papers and court rulings for those buildings to be demolished. And all the legal remedies had been fulfilled, and the decisions had come into force. Some of these decisions we inherited, as I say, and others were made by us ourselves. So at that period of time it is a fact that some 60 facilities were destroyed. I say "facilities" intentionally because some of them were chicken coops, and others were buildings. They weren't all houses and dwellings. So I say "facilities." That's the term I use.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And those facilities, did they belong to Serbs only or to whom did they belong?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: That's the point. They did not belong to Serbs. They also belonged to Croats and Muslims and Serbs, to all three. That was what it was quite certainly and nothing else. So it was only a question of whether they could be legalised or not. Those that could not be legalised, that is, a small portion of those facilities were demolished. And as I say, there were about 60 of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was a rally held in the summer of 1991 at the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. A rally was held, but I don't think it was in the summer. I think it was in the spring. I think it was April when the rally was held at Ivanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please answer the questions very briefly so we can conduct this.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: My answer is yes. It was held at Ivanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who conducted the rally and who attended it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The rally was held under the SDS organisation from Trebinje. However, participation in the rally included other parties. We had the representatives of the popular party from Montenegro, for example. Then representatives of the SDS turned up from, I think -- I think there was an SDS representative from Knin as well. But I can't say with certainty. I do sort of remember that he might have been. And also from other Serb parties, we saw representatives arriving there, too. Now, I have to say in addition that in the statement that I gave and which I leafed through yesterday, I saw that an error had been made, a typing error. The SDS means the Serbian Democratic Party. At the same time, the SDS and the abbreviation for the State Security Service, that is, also SDS. So when I talked to the investigator in Dubrovnik, he ranked those people and joined them up to the SDS party. But the two have nothing to do with each other. So would you please take that into account. It is not the same something.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I do not need to go into the details of who was member of the SDS party. But if I understand you correctly, when you reviewed your previous interview, statement, you noticed that there was a passage in there where the SDS party and the police department was confused. That is what you want to correct here, but we do not need to go into these details.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the rally, what was the gist of the rally? What was the message coming from this rally?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The message was the same as all the other messages that were put forward at that particular time in the spring of 1991. There were intensive preparations underway for everything that was to happen in the near future so that all the speeches uttered at the rally, and you have them on the tape, were along those lines. They were intoned in that way. They were very war like with respect to the Croatian side. They were very belligerent with respect to the fact that democracy had come to Croatia, and that Croatia quite certainly would no longer be in the situation it had previously been in. And there were overtones according to which the question of the protection of Serb rights in those regions were highlighted, in this case, in Dubrovnik. And I'm not quite sure as to what was to be defended or protected there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the time of this rally and the time leading up to the war, were the Serbs in any way endangered in their position in Dubrovnik as part of the population, their rights?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know of a single case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatian population or authorities pose a threat to the JNA in the region at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatian authorities at that time deploy army or special police forces in Dubrovnik region in the direction of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in that summer, in Konavle, which is that reach towards the -- towards Montenegro, it is the southernmost part, there were four policemen. If truth be told, in the place called Cilipi from June onwards, there was an organised company of the Croatian National Guard Corps. But that same company was demobilised; that is to say, it ceased to exist. It was disbanded in the month of that August of that same year, 1991. So that they were actually there from June until August, but not after that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did the few policemen that you mentioned or anyone else in this region, did they attack Montenegro or shoot or shell into Montenegrin territory? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No, quite certainly, quite definitely no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did JNA troops, on the other hand, shoot and shell into the Dubrovnik municipality from Bosnia or Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The provocations through shooting began as early on as September, around the 10th or 12th of September, in fact. What happened was that from the hill called Kobile, and that is the border line between Croatia and Montenegro, the eastern half belongs to Montenegro, the western reaches belongs to Croatia, so this western area was in Konavle, and it was from that hill that there was intensive firing coming at the population of Konavle. And on one occasion, I was present when this took place. I was in a place called Vitalina in front of a restaurant, rather a village inn, a typical village inn. And that is what is the southern most part in the Konavle area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you speak of September, you speak of 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned the rally, the rally. And I would like to know if during this rally and in the time that came afterwards, was there any talk about a Dubrovnik republic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was any talk of that at the rally in April. I can't confirm that. I'd have to look through the tapes. So I can't actually assert that there was talk of that at the rally itself. However, after the Serbo/Montenegrin army arrived and took control of Konavle, it was then that their project to set up the Dubrovnik republic became intensive. They even set up a board for the restoration of that so called Dubrovnik republic, and the board was headed by a prominent man called Aco Apolonjo, who for many years was the public Prosecutor in Dubrovnik. And as far as I know, there were eight members in that board or council, and they held several meetings in Cavtat, in the town of Cavtat, but nothing actually came of it. Or rather, they did not succeed in what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Dubrovnik republic, what was that supposed to mean? What was understood by this Dubrovnik republic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, the Dubrovnik republic had existed. It ceased to exist in 1806, 1808. And from those days onwards, it has no longer existed. It stretched from the borders at Neum up until Sutorina, and it was to have meant that this newly established or reinstated Dubrovnik republic, according to them, was to have been reliant on what would be outside the borders of the republic which would mean the new Serbia, that is to say Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 14399 to 14411. Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness, and it is tab 1 of the exhibit binder designed for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give it a number, the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The two binders will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 361.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you see here it is a pamphlet of a movement for the Dubrovnik republic. And it speaks here of a restoration of a modern demilitarised and democratic Dubrovnik republic. And it refers also in the header to the citizens of all areas of the former Yugoslavia. This document, were you aware of this movement and do you know which person is standing behind it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of the movement. I knew about it. And I had in my hands this piece of paper at one time. This is how it was. And it was the Council for the Restoration of the Dubrovnik Republic. And as far as I know, Mr. Aco Apolonjo headed that council. I don't know whether he's still alive. Some people say he is; some people say he isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those in the movement for the Dubrovnik republic, were they Serbs or of all sorts of ethnicities? Can you say that? And were they related to the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: For the most part, they were Serbs. Now, what their links were with the SDS party, I cannot say, but yes the majority were Serbs. And as far as I know, there was a Croat amongst them, however, that particular Croat was a man whose conduct was, mildly speaking, strange. That's what I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said already that this Dubrovnik republic would be out of -- outside of the Croatian republic and part of a new Serbia. Was that propagated by this movement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before the war broke out, did you try to make contact with the JNA to avoid the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on several occasions. Not just I, but the Prime Minister, that is, the president of the municipal government, Mr. Sikic. We wanted several times to get in touch with them, and several times we managed to achieve contact with them. I would like to say that in that misfortune, it was lucky that -- it was fortunate that the commander of the Boka military district was, in my view, a normal person who, unfortunately, is now deceased. His name was Krsto Djuruvic. At the time, he was captain of a frigate. Later on, he was promoted to the rank of admiral. Ex officio, he was member of the Council for the Protection of Dubrovnik Municipality, and we frequently discussed problems. And once, in Kupari, we went there as a delegation, and they were there also as the collocutors on the other side. But the second time, it was in Herceg Novi, but by then it was clearly too late to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tell me, when did you visit Admiral Djuruvic in Herceg Novi?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I think this was around the 15th or the 16th of September. I'm unable to say exactly, but anyway, one of those two days. And I spoke to them in the army centre there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On your way to Herceg Novi and around the army centre, did you see JNA troops or other military troops gather?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I did. There were many soldiers. They were mostly reservists. One could tell by their age and their attire and the fact that they were not very neatly dressed that they were mostly reservists already deployed at several positions. These military fortifications were being made, and one could already feel that war was at our doorstep.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Admiral Djuruvic the situation, especially the presence of these troops on the Montenegrin side?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did he tell you why they were there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: At the time, he was in a special sort of mood. He said that they were there exclusively to defend themselves. Unfortunately, we were not alone. There was a person who was listening to everything, probably recording as well - he didn't say anything except on one occasion - and I realised that Mr. Djuruvic was unable to tell me what he really thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Defend themselves against whom? Did he say that? Did he speak --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I asked him that, in fact. And he said that they had information that, on our side, that there were a large number of troops with who knows what kind of conquering aspirations towards Montenegro and the Bay of Kotor. All this sounded rather ridiculous to me, and he was aware that that was so but I had the feeling that he had to say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you tell him that this was not correct, and that there were no troops on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I told him, and just then, this other person who was listening joined in the conversation, claiming that in the St. Anne church at Brgat, there was an Ustasha nest which they have to destroy at all costs. I let him speak, and when he finished, I said to him: "Listen, sir, at the St. Anne church, there is no belfry," because he mentioned the bell tower, that there was an Ustasha nest in the bell tower. And indeed, there was no bell tower nor was there any nest there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Admiral Djuruvic make any promises to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Admiral Djuruvic, throughout that time, was obviously waiting for a chance to tell me just one sentence. And at the end, when he was sure that nobody could hear it except me, he said: "While I'm the commander of this district, you can rest assured that not a single shell will fall on Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was Mr. -- was Admiral Djuruvic replaced?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: A couple of days later, he was in some sort of detention, and then he was released. He was again at his post for two days, and then he was killed. The opposing party claimed that we had killed him, but it was clear to me that we hadn't killed him because there were no troops of ours on the spot where he was killed, and it was immediately clear to me that this must have been some combinations on their part. And eventually, I really did find out that they had killed him. Much later, much later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you find out and what did you find out in relation to this killing? But very briefly.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I was told by a person who was on their side and who carried him from the helicopter to a vehicle in a dying condition - he was unconscious and he was dying - and he told me the details about the incident. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And according to this information, "they" killed him, meaning who?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Meaning the Serbian/Montenegrin army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who came afterwards? Who was in charge after his death?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic came.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know when he became the commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, Djuruvic was killed on the 4th of October. So I assume that Admiral Jokic took over on that same date, or maybe the next day, on the 5th. I can't say. But I met him when he was already in that position on the 11th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I would like to hear more details about the incident which the witness heard from the third person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Um-hum, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As you heard, the Judge would like to hear more details about how Admiral Djuruvic was killed and by whom.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: In all truth, I cannot say because I didn't see it. I'm just passing on what this man told him who was there when the helicopter was landing, and not falling. He wasn't killed in the helicopter because the helicopter fell. It is true that the helicopter landed in a rather unusual way. This did not happen in the village of Popovici in Konavle, as was announced, but rather, 150 metres southeast from Vukobrat glass houses that were also in Konavle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: According to what you were told, was the helicopter shot down?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: According to what this man said, the helicopter was flying in a rather strange way, but he didn't hear anyone opening fire at the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did Djuruvic die?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: When that man ran up to the helicopter, he was outside the helicopter, and he was dying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you just try and concentrate on the question, Mr. Poljanic, please. If you don't know how he died, just say so. But if you do know, could you tell us briefly what -- how he came to die.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how he was killed, but I know that he died. But how and who killed him, I don't know. Who the person was who killed him, whether he killed himself, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the war, did you go to Trebinje to meet with Bozidar Vucurevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you go there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: This was round about that time, two or three days after that. I went to Trebinje for a conversation --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said two or three days after that. After what? When did you go there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: After this incident when I spoke to Mr. Djuruvic in Herceg Novi. He was still, of course, alive then. So this could have been on the 17th or 18th of September. Yes, 17 or 18th of September, I went to talk to Mr. Vucurevic in Trebinje. We had information that in Trebinje, there was a strong concentration of troops, that next to the road from Trebinje towards the Croatian border, there were again strong forces ready to attack. And I went to talk to him to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see this concentration of troops when you went to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I saw them on the road to Trebinje and in Trebinje itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Trebinje is how far away from Dubrovnik approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: 27 kilometres by road. Much less as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a garrison there or barracks, and if so --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And which military facility was it? Was there a corps stationed, or what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The infantry to be quite frank, I am not very familiar with various military units, corps and brigades. I know, however, that there were 6.000-odd soldiers in the barracks at the time, before the attack on Dubrovnik and around it, there were many more. Now, whether that's a brigade or a corps, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was your information in relation to 6.000 soldiers being there? How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The commander of the barracks in Trebinje was Mr. Nojko Marinovic, in those days a Lieutenant-Colonel in the Yugoslav army, a Croat from the surroundings of Benkovac. And we had certain information about what was going on in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This lieutenant-colonel, did he subsequently become the commander of the Croatian defenders of Dubrovnik? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He went over to our side in Dubrovnik, and as soon as he did that, and that was on the 18th or 19th of September in 1991, he took over as the leader of the defence of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Vucurevic. What was his position at that time? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the municipality of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he have political views in relation to Dubrovnik? Did he ever express anything? Did he tell you something?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, in that conversation of ours, I must admit that he did not express any major pretensions towards the territory of Dubrovnik municipality. Of course, I told him with respect to the situation I had seen along the road, that is, the large concentration of troops, I told him that I found all this surprising because we have absolutely no ambitions, nor ability, to wage war for anybody's territory. But that if anything were to happen, we would defend our territory to the best of our ability. And he just said to me at one point literally: "Well, we're only interested in that little bit further to the south." That's literally what he said. He didn't express any other pretensions in the course of that conversation which went on for two or three hours. We even had a walk together through Trebinje for the people in the streets to see that we had no -- there were no hostilities between us, at least not on my part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This "little bit further to the south," does that refer to a part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Absolutely a part of Croatia, and this could have meant only Konavle, because that is the southern most area of Croatia. Whether he meant a part of Konavle or the whole of Konavle, I really don't know what he had in mind because he didn't tell me and it wouldn't be fair for me to say. I just repeated the sentence that he uttered.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Vucurevic was close to Radovan Karadzic? Do you know anything to this effect?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I do know that he frequently mentioned in that conversation, Radovan said this to me, Radovan said that to me, and Slobo said this, and Slobo said that. So I assumed that he meant, when he mentioned Radovan, that he meant Radovan Karadzic, and when he used the word "Slobo," that he meant Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the conversation about when he referred to Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Milosevic, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: In that conversation between him and me, there was nothing alarming. In fact, I had the feeling that through that conversation, he wanted to indicate to me that he was on good terms with both of them. I don't even remember exactly what he mentioned as having talked about with Karadzic and Milosevic, if they are the persons he meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Vucurevic, despite this conversation with you, did he express political views in relation to Yugoslavia and Dubrovnik on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: On other occasions, yes; very frequently, in fact. He always spoke about the protection of Serb interests in the areas which were not a component part of Serbia. In his reflections and activities and the vocabulary he used, he was very, very malignant. And also there is his well-known sentence once the war started and when Dubrovnik lived through the greatest catastrophe in its history: "So what? We will rebuild Dubrovnik to make it even more beautiful and even newer." Something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was a naval blockade imposed on Dubrovnik region on the 30th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the region attacked the next day, 1st October?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, could you tell us what the reason or the pretext, as you may put it, was for the JNA's attack at the time? Was there any ultimatum or any notice or something like that before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the attack, no. Before the attack, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you know at the later stage the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason could only have been one, but as far as the ultimatum is concerned, we did get ultimatums later, but not up to that point in time. The reason could have been Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik area and Konavle - which let me add in passing is 100 per cent ethnically Croatian - was the road towards the west, eventually towards Karlobag where their border was meant to be, even though that is 400 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the ultimatum like?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have the documents actually here, and I would come to this in the course of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the aim of the attack? You mentioned "their border." What does that refer to and what was the aim of the attack in the long term?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, you see the aim of the attack on the 1st of October when the worst we had experienced up to then happened - later on, it was even worse - the aim was to block us entirely, to separate us, to deprive us of electricity, water, and any communication with the world. All the television transmitters were destroyed, the transformer station in Komoljac. The water supply installations were destroyed. We were left without electricity, without water, without telephone lines, without TV programmes, without the ability to communicate by road or by sea. So just then, we were probably the largest prison in the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I had referred to your quote "eventually towards Karlobag where their border was meant to be." I was actually asking you what do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the fact how would they form the border at Karlobag unless they conquer everything leading to Karlobag and Split and Sibenik and Zadar. But they didn't attack Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean the municipality of Dubrovnik lies in a territory that would be part of Serbia or Yugoslavia or the new Yugoslavia that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Certainly. You see, these people who committed provocations in Croatia would chant slogans "This will be Serbia" and all their other well-known songs. So these were agents provocateurs

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the atlas. This is Exhibit 336, and the pages 36 and 37. And I would like to have it put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you point to us the regions that were attacked and taken. In the municipality of Dubrovnik, of course.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The southernmost point in Croatia is Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you please show Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Here it is, exactly here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you please show us the entire region that was taken over and attacked on the 1st of October and the subsequent days.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: As my pointer is going, this is the area of Konavle, right up to Cavtat, including Cavtat, up to Ljuta, in fact. All of this is Konavle. Then comes the Dubrovnik Zupa, then the town of Dubrovnik itself. Then from Zaton you have the Dubrovnik coast which goes as literal -- goes as far as the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina at Neum. This is the Dubrovnik literal. Over here is Peljesac, which was also part of Dubrovnik municipality. The island of Mljet, then the islands of Kolocep, Lopud, and Sipan. All of this is Dubrovnik municipality. And in Peljesac, it went as far as the place called Postup.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And from which directions did the troops attack and take over? Can you show that as well.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I can. The area of Dubrovnik was attacked from the south, across Debeli Brijeg, then from Herzegovina via Dubravka, a locality in Konavle, then from Trebinje, also towards Dubrovnik, and from Popovo Polje via Zavala, they reached Slano. This was on the 4th. And they also arrived here, to the Dubrovnik literal, through Cepikuca. And of course, crossing all the other hills there but not in such large numbers. These were the main axes of attack, and of course from the sea. And all this was accompanied by attacks by the navy which was no more merciful than the army, and also the air force was involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in -- which troops were they? Were they JNA, TO, or what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: They were -- they said they were the JNA, though they had various insignia. As far as I know, the JNA had on their caps a five-cornered star. In those days, those insignia were very different, so there were not just five-cornered stars on their caps but various other insignia as well. I don't know how I could call them, whether that army could still be called the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how much time did these troops need to take over the territory that you showed to us on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: This heavy attack started on the 1st of October. Konavle, up until the 12th of the afternoon, including Cavtat, were captured by the 12th in the afternoon. On the 4th of October, Slano was taken. And then they went from Slano towards the south, so one after another there was localities that fell: Maravinci, Brsecine, Orasac, Zaton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you just concentrate, please, on the question. It was a simple question. How long did it take for them to take over the territory? Can you just give us an idea in terms of days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Konavle, it took them from the 1st of October until the 12th of October. For the Dubrovnik literal, a little longer, a couple of days longer. But the Dubrovnik literal attack started on the 4th and not on the 1st. Slano fell on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So it took approximately 12 days, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the result of this attack, were Croatian villages in this area that you just showed to us destroyed or severely damaged?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: It was exclusively Croatian villages that were in that area, and some of them were almost completely destroyed. For example, in that Konavle area, some villages were completely destroyed, others partially destroyed. But at any rate, Konavle experienced the greatest tragedy in its history and the greatest destruction of its history. The place called Cilipi was almost 100 per cent destroyed. Benkovac was destroyed 100 per cent. Gruda almost 100 per cent, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me put to you some villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And actually, Your Honours, it's the villages listed in paragraph 81 of the Croatia indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to you to comment on each of these villages whether you know they were destroyed and the amount of destruction. Very briefly, no details. Brgat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago Zvekovica was completely destroyed. And where there were some 30 or 40 houses left standing after Konavle were liberated, we just found a mass of rubble, not a single house was left standing, not a single wall was left standing. Cilipi was also almost completely destroyed. And Mocici, a little hamlet between Cilipi and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to put to you the names of villages, and you just comment on this particular village, please. Brgat, was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Very well. Brgat? You mean Brgat, I assume. Is that what you mean, Brgat? Yes, Brgat was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Cilipi you already mentioned. Dubravka?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Dubravka is a place in Konavle. Yes, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Grude.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Grude, the largest place after Cavtat, yes, terribly destroyed and demolished. Not absolutely 100 per cent of the houses, but let's say 80 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mocici.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Mocici, just like Cilipi, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Osojnik.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Osojnik is not in Konavle. That is a place right above Mokosica, up in the hills. It is a place which was destroyed 100 per cent. I think of the 103 houses, 102 were completely demolished. One was left standing where the army -- where the soldiers lived, and they didn't succeed in destroying that when they left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Soldiers -- you said, where soldiers lived. What soldiers? Croatian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No, no. The Serb/Montenegrin army. The Serb/Montenegrin army. That's who it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean they took over this building and stayed there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think you already mentioned Slano. Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned Slano. Slano is a beautiful place on the coast in a little bay, and there were a lot of beautiful villas there. It was totally, absolutely totally destroyed, including the hotels.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Popovici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you help me find the place on the map, Slano.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at the atlas again on the ELMO and point out Slano.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: It's here. It's in the Dubrovnik literal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. And the next place is Donja Ljuta. If you would also whenever you speak about a place, point it out on the map.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So Donja Ljuta.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: There is a Ljuta in Konavle, and another Ljuta bay where the hydroelectric power plant emerges. Do you know the Konavle Ljuta? Is that the place you mean? You probably mean the Konavle Ljuta because it is a village there, and that was destroyed, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. So it's in Konavle. And the next one is Popovici.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Popovici, that is another place in Konavle. A lot of it was destroyed, but as far as I remember, not completely. Not like Cilipi, Zvekovica, Mihanici, Dubravka and the other places were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about Mihanici?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mihanici, Konavle, yes, they were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Drvenik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Drvenik. Yes, also in Konavle and was also demolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Plat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Plat is a place in the Dubrovnik literal once again. Not in the Dubrovnik literal, but in the Dubrovacka Zupa county, and Plat was also damaged to a great extent including all the hotels that existed in Plat. Not only were they destroyed but they were looted, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Cepikuce?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Cepikuce is a place in the Dubrovnik literal, on the coast. It was destroyed, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Uskoplje?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Uskoplje, I think you mean. In the Konavle, area. Yes, that was destroyed, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Gabrili?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Gabrili, that is a place in Konavle once again. And yes, it was destroyed heavily.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Pridvorje?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Pridvorje is a place also in Konavle near Gabrili with a wonderful old monastery, and it was quite considerably damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Molunat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Molunat is a place in Konavle along the coast. It was damaged, but not nearly like the places we've mentioned just now. Although there was great destruction there, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Donja Cibaca?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I think you mean Donja Cibaca. Donja Cibaca is a place in the Dubrovacka Zupa under Dubac. And the place was very heavily damaged. Yes, heavily damaged, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Karasovici?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Karasovici are a border place in Konavle, along the border between Montenegro and Croatia. And that's where the border crossing of Debeli Brijeg is to this day. That place, too, was significantly damaged and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the last place, Zvekovica, you have already mentioned as being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Zvekovica, completely destroyed. Completely. I don't know if there is a single house left standing in Zvekovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you meet with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in preparation of your testimony, and did you review, on this occasion, a huge stack of documentation with photos of damage to these places?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you provide a declaration confirming the correctness of the documentations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. To all photographs that I looked at, and there are very many of them, I gave a written statement saying that they were true and authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, as tab 3 of the exhibit, we have this declaration. It was prepared, and it is signed by the witness. And following this declaration are actually, starting with tab 4 going on through to Tab 32, photographs of the places that are indicated in the declaration. And rather than putting it to the witness during this testimony, we have prepared the declaration referring to what he reviewed during the preparation. And the Prosecution would like to tender it as a stack into evidence. It's photos --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit the declaration and the exhibits which are referred to in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in these photos that you saw of the damaged location, did you also see photos with ethnically based, anti-Croat graffiti?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the translation of this graffiti is also included in the specific tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I feel that the Court ought to bear in mind that on none of these photographs is there the date as to when the photograph was taken. I think that the Prosecution should explain how we're going to ascertain when the photographs were actually taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, when you reviewed the documentation, was it actually documentation produced by the police station in -- of the Dubrovnik-Neretva police department, and do these reports indicate when they were produced?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to point Your Honours to actually the reports where it always indicates on the first page the date when the report was made. It's most -- it states from -- mostly it is the 6th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, those damages that you saw in the documentation, do you know when these villages were destroyed? Not the exact day, but the time period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: As to the exact date, I cannot tell you for certain. But I can tell you for certain that all the photographs - and I saw hundreds of them shown to me by you, perhaps even more - all of them to the last relate to the period after, or rather, during the destruction of the Dubrovnik region. The photographs were taken after these territories were liberated, of course. Now exactly when, I can't say. I can't give you a date.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the closest that we can come to the date when the photographs were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's now 12.15. Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Poljanic, would you remember, please, during this adjournment and any others there may be not to speak to anybody about your evidence, and that does include the Prosecution team, until it's over. Thank you. 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have just briefly addressed the graffiti that were seen on photos. Did you see photos with graffiti indicating names of many persons and places from Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just as examples, you find this in tab 13, tab 16, tab 20, and tab 23 as examples, without addressing them now or here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did any of the destroyed villages that we just spoke about, did any of these villages have military installations of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were JNA facilities in that region? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The JNA had some facilities on the island of Mljet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But that's not in the villages --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No, that's not in any one of the villages that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did actual fighting take place while these villages were taken over and damaged or destroyed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No. There was some -- in Konavle, a few young men who were organised, when the Yugoslav army arrived and started with its occupation, occupying places towards Cavtat, I think in Pridvorje, there was a clash of some kind that broke out, but I can't actually confirm that. I seem to remember that there were some sporadic shooting there, but nobody was either injured or killed in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware of any casualties of the JNA side during these takeover and attacks on the region?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that in Konavle, anybody died on the side of the JNA except for the man that we said was dead, Admiral Djuruvic, but we don't know how he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to these other two regions, Zupa Dubravka and Primorje, is that different from Konavle?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in the Dubrovacka Zupa, the Dubrovnik county, that there was some resistance. Now, how many dead on the side of the Yugoslav army, I don't know. On our side, there were people killed, quite a number of them. Innocent people - not soldiers - civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When these villages were attacked, what actually happened to the Croatian population living in there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about Konavle or Zupa?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's talk about Konavle first.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Konavle moved out practically everyone. Perhaps just 5 per cent stayed on, and they were elderly men and women. Elderly persons, very old people stayed. But otherwise, all the rest left. They left Konavle, they left their homes. And for the most part came to Dubrovnik. I remember that they were mostly accommodated in the Babin Kuk area, and some of them went to the northern Dalmatian coastline to, the islands, and there are a lot of refugees from Dubrovnik, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say they left their homes, what does it mean? Does it mean they fled or in which way did they leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: They fled in the throws of the shelling, the beating, and the burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: About how many people are we talking here in relation to Konavle, how many people fled?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, Konavle numbered, as far as I remember, in 1990, 8.200, I think, inhabitants, thereabouts. Now, if we agreed upon the fact that 5 per cent remain, then you can calculate what that figure is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many people left or fled from the Primorje region?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Almost all of them, from the villages that were occupied. There were some villages from which few people left. But villages like Cepikuce, Lisac, Tocionik, Trnova, which was completely destroyed, the entire population left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many are there in numbers all together?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Several thousand inhabitants, a couple of thousand inhabitants left from the Dubrovacka/Primorje.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And from Zupa Dubrovacka, this region, how many people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Almost all of them. Also several thousand inhabitants, which is the number of inhabitants that the Dubrovacka Zupa had. Very few of them remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did anything happen to those who remained?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this. When they arrived in Mlini, they killed everybody that they found there. For example, at the doors of the hotel, the director was killed. And several other people were killed, and the others fled regardless.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "they," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The Serb/Montenegrin army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were people detained?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. People were detained from Konavle, those who had not succeeded in escaping and were captured. Other people from Zupa were detained, who were captured and detained who had not succeeded from escaping from the Dubrovnik/Primorje area, too. And for the most part they were taken off to the camp in Morinje in Montenegro. And a portion, most of those from the Dubrovnik/Primorje, they were taken off to Bileca. But there were no specific rules as to that. Some of them from the Dubrovnik/Primorje were also taken to the Morinje camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Morinje camp in Montenegro, was this a JNA facility?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of facility was it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say what kind. It was a military facility. There were three low typical military buildings. What they were used for before, I don't know, nor do I understand what they are used for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many people from the region were detained there and for -- in which time period? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of October when this all started until the end of December when an exchange took place, about 300 persons from the Dubrovnik area were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Bileca. Is this a JNA facility or what kind of place were people detained in there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know how many people from detained there from the region, not from other places, and for how long, in which time period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: From the Dubrovnik area alone, there were less people there than in Morinje. And they stayed on longer, a little longer than the ones in Morinje did. A little longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say less people, did you give a number of people who were from your region taken there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I allow for the possibility of making a mistake in quoting a figure, but I don't think there were more than about 150 from the area. Not more than that, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what is your information on this detention, from where did you get the information that 300 persons were detained in Morinje and maybe 150 in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Of the people who were there -- from the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean you met them afterwards when they returned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I met many of them, many of them were my friends. And of course, many of them told me about the atrocities that they had experienced there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Atrocities, what kind of atrocities did -- were committed in Morinje? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: People were tortured in amazing ways, and I think that you will have a man here who was actually there, so he will be able to tell you more about that. So I would rather not speak about that issue. It's too sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In -- I would like to put tab 33 of 361 to the witness. And it is a proclamation to the citizens from the 7th of November, 1991, of the Cavtat town command and the Cavtat local commune committee. And first of all, the Cavtat town command, what kind of command is it? Is it a military command, and of which --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Exclusively the military command.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And of which army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Of the Serb/Montenegrin army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the Cavtat local commune committee, what is it? What kind of a body was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Those people who, up until the time the place was occupied, who were there, mostly ended up in Morinje. And then a body of their own was set up which sort of coordinated or did what it could under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it says here in the -- actually the first paragraph, the bigger paragraph, it says: "The town command and JNA units have partially finalised the cleansing of the area, detained a part of the remaining military formations' members, and collected some weapons, ammunition, explosives, with your assistance and collaboration." Do you know which people from Cavtat were detained; and if so, were they part of military formations of the Croatian army? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know of a single person who was detained from Cavtat and ended up in Morinje having been a member of any kind of military formation. I know about some who ended up there who were activists in this local board and Crisis Staff, local committee and Crisis Staff. As to any soldier, I really don't know that there were any.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In relation to the detainees that you mentioned in Morinje and Bileca, do you know whether they were civilians or soldiers or both?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Mostly they were civilians. There were just a few soldiers in Bileca. Now, some were transferred from Bileca to Morinje, so I don't want to say that there was not a single soldier in Morinje. I do know that some were transferred to Morinje. But of the 300 people in Morinje, very few of them were soldiers. Not more than, let's say, a fifth. Mostly they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have already spoken about the destructions and handed in the documentation. Do you know whether these places and these villages were looted? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I do know that they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that? Who did it and how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Exclusively, the army that was there, they took everything that was mobile, or at least most of what could be moved, what they were interested in. They carried away from Konavle what hadn't burned down. They also carried away from Zupa what hadn't burned, especially from the hotel. They carried off property from the literal and all the hotels along the coast, and they also carried off a large number of vessels from the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to Dubrovnik town itself. In which time period was it shelled? Can you say? When it started, and we are concentrating on the year 1991.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I think before I start my answer to that question, we should make it quite clear that when I refer to Dubrovnik, I'm referring to the whole town. And when I'm thinking of the protected old city that is under UNESCO protection, I will refer to it as the old town. So my answer is when the attack on Dubrovnik started, it is the 1st of October. If you're asking me when the shelling of the old city started, then my answer is the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to give to the witness a map, the map of the town, actually. And this would need to be inserted into the map binder which has the Exhibit Number 326, and it would become an additional tab, tab 13. You have a rather small map while, on the ELMO, we have now a bigger one. But we will provide a better copy on a later date. We were not in a position to make a better one in the time period that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, would you please point out to us on the map the old town Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: This is it that I am encircling with the pointer. That is the old town of Dubrovnik. That is the protected old city.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Protected in which way?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: As part of the world cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on the other part of the map, that's all the entire town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. The whole town of Dubrovnik is shown. But maybe the most beautiful part is to the right of the old town, the area known as Ploce, as far as the Belvedere Hotel, which is not shown on this map but I can show it to you if we open up the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, not at the moment. You mentioned also hotels where refugees from the region actually were placed. Can you show this on the map, where they were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The refugees were mostly accommodated in all the hotels, but most of them in Babin Kuk. This is this area here coloured in black ink, those buildings there. And the Libertas Hotel, which is right here, that I am pointing to now. Of course, some were accommodated in other hotels as well, but most of them in these two places.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And to put the map aside for a moment, but you can leave it there on the ELMO, you mentioned already that the town was shelled beginning on the 1st of October, and how long did it continue to be shelled? I mean, the entire town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought the evidence was it was the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, the old town, Your Honour. I was speaking about Dubrovnik town, the shelling of the entire region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The entire region was shelled from the 1st until when? In 1991. We'll concentrate on 1991.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it lasted, with interruptions, virtually up until the liberation of the whole area. However, in actual fact, it went on until the summer of 1995 because it would not be fair not to mention that the last shell fell in August 1995 and killed three innocent people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I had asked you to concentrate on the year 1991. And what would be the end date for the shelling of Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The 31st of December, because continuously, not on a daily basis, true, there are records about this, but Dubrovnik was intensively shelled, in particular, in mid-November. And there was an exceptionally heavy shelling on the 10th and 11th, and especially the 12th of November. And then every couple of days, there would be more shelling. Not as intensively as on the 12th, but a shell or two would be fired. The areas outside the old city were more heavily shelled in that time period, but the old city also would regularly be hit by one or two shells. And the culmination was on the 6th of December when a really disastrous destruction occurred, by far the greatest in the history not only of Dubrovnik, but of the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the old town, you said, started to get shelled on the 23rd of October and also through to the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the 23rd, you mean. The 23rd, only two shells fell. And then after that, a couple of days later, many more, then many more, then less, then more. Then in mid-November, it peaked, there were very many then. Several hundred. And if you want the total number of shells on the old city, and I must tell you that there is a record of each and every shell that fell on the old city, I think the number is 1.056, on the old city.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said already that in November 10, 11, and 12 was intensive shelling on both the town as such and the old town. And on --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Of the whole town and the old town, yes, precisely so. But there was also shelling between mid-November and the 6th of December. But not so intensively, but shelling all the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. From where was Dubrovnik and also the old town, from where was it targeted? From which positions? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: From the positions of Zarkovica, from Grab, from Strincera, from the position at Miocic, from positions of the western part of the airstrip in Cilipi, from Brgat, as far as these positions were concerned. As for the positions from which Slano and Sipan were shelled, those were positions in the immediate vicinity just behind Slano, on the road leading from Slano towards Orahov Do, Zorovo, Ravno. They had positions there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I was actually asking only from where Dubrovnik was shelled and was not talking about Slano, shells on Slano. Let's -- we are speak now about Dubrovnik only.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put Exhibit 361, tab 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, is this a photo of Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and can you indicate on this photo the point Zarkovica that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: The picture was taken precisely from the Zarkovica position, so whoever was taking the photograph was standing at a spot known as Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From Zarkovica, did you have an unobstructed view on the old town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Absolutely unobstructed. With the exception of the Gruz harbour, which is the harbour of Dubrovnik. You can't see Gruz from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is indicated on the photo also Babin Kuk where you mentioned the hotels and the Libertas Hotel. Would that be positioned correct here on this photo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Babin Kuk is marked correctly, but Libertas not quite, not quite correctly, but it was lower down than this red spot. So that is where Libertas is, but roughly speaking, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the old town and also Dubrovnik as such, was it also shelled from ships?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you know from which -- would this map here or this photograph, would that be correct as -- in regard to the shelling from ships?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we can put this --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Except, let me note. Here on this map, on this photograph, I can't see the directions of shelling from ships towards the Ploce area, and this is the Ploce area, and shelling from boats to Ploce was quite intensive. Also, to the left, in the left-hand corner, is the Belvedere Hotel which was for days shelled from boats. It cannot be seen on this photograph, nor can you see the direction from the boats towards it. So this would be the only omission on this photograph, if one could call it that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Witness, was the old town shelled indiscriminately, or were specific buildings targeted? Do you know that? Could you observe anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: My impression is that buildings were not targeted, because the old town, the whole of the old town was shelled on the 7th of December when I climbed on to the ramparts, the walls. Unfortunately, I couldn't find a single roof on which a shell had not fallen or had been destroyed by the shell falling on the roof next door. So my conclusion is that they didn't have specific targets; the target was the town itself. I mean the old town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not like to go into details of the damage done to the old town because we will have a witness, the witness Franic who was actually already mentioned as a witness. And this witness is actually an expert at the same time as an eyewitness, and he would speak about the damage. And we do not need to have it twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, just -- you mentioned already that almost each building was -- each roof was at least damaged, and you are referring to the shelling on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Not just the 6th of December, but also on the 6th of December roofs were damaged before that, too. But not as badly as on the 6th of December and not to such an extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, what I would like to talk to you about is actually the casualties, if there were any, in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And for this, to assist in this, I would like to put to the witness tab 35 of the Exhibit 361. And it's actually the annex to the indictment, to the Croatia indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did you have opportunity to review this document while you had your conversation here in The Hague with members of the Prosecutors' Office, including me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You see here the people listed with dates. Could you say whether these people listed in the annex were killed on that day, on the days indicated and in the places indicated? Is the list in so far correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware that these people were killed, and what was your information to that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among them, some were my friends. I learned on the same day they were killed. I would learn about their deaths. They were reported to me. I even buried some of those on this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So does it mean the list from the beginning, 1st October, with Mato Violic, down to the 6th December, Ilija Radic, is correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those persons listed here, were they civilians or soldiers or both? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I cannot say whether there were any soldiers among them. Perhaps among those I didn't know. But regarding all those that I knew from this list, not a single one of them was a soldier. Possibly among those I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you point out those you know, or -- point out those you knew that were civilians. Can you do that. Just say the name going down the list.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: You want me to read out the names?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Mato Violic, for instance, was a civilian. I knew him extremely well. Milan Milisic, a writer. Stijepo Cikato, Jozo Brajovic. The Liban brothers. Maskaric. Bokun.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Both or?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Both persons, both. Bruno Glanc. Pavo Urban. Those are the names that I have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And among those killed on the 6th of December, are there fire workers among them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before I answer that question, I noticed here there are a couple of soldiers. I see now that there were a couple of soldiers, people who were soldiers. Yes, please. What was your next question?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First, you haven't answered. First, will you please answer my question in relation to fire workers. Whether among those killed on the 6th of December, were there any fire workers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the point in time when the Libertas Hotel which was full of refugees was burning. After many shells had hit it, it was up in flames. And several firefighters went to try and save the people. Among them was this young man that I just mentioned, Bruno Glanc. A shell hit them and killed each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who are the others? Are they also on the list, the other fire workers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I think that they are these Jablan, Paskojevic, Mihocevic. I think that is the group. I think there were five of them in the group. Three of them were active-duty firefighters, and two joined them to assist them, and all five were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you just saw that on the list there are several soldiers. Who would they be? Can you give the names?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I think -- I think that Ivo Martinovic was a soldier. I think so. If he's the one I have in mind, then he was a soldier. But it may be another Martinovic. But I think he was a soldier. Then this young man, yes, he was a soldier. If he's the one I'm thinking of, unless it's somebody with the same name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I think it's the one I'm thinking of. Ivo Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is born 1915?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, that can't be the one. I'm sorry. Oh, I see, 1915 -- no, no, this was a young man, a young Martinovic. I'm not even sure that his first name was Ivo, but I do know that his surname was Martinovic and I know he was killed at Srdj, but it's out of the question that he could be the one as he was born in 1915, so I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, among those that --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: In that case, there's not a single soldier among these on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... is not listed here, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness tab 36 of the Exhibit 361. And I only -- only this one.
