utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention just to one article.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Your Honours, it's page 7 of the English translation, and it's an article with the headline "Tragic Consequences of the 6th December --" there is a mistake in the translation. It says 6th September but it's 6th December -- "Attack."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you see here listed, actually, those we find in the annex listed under the 6th of December, and we, in addition, find here mentioned the following: "Courageous defenders of Dubrovnik and the members of National Guard Corps, Marko Bitunjac, Nenad Covic, Mario Zelenika, Saban Islamoski, and Miroslav Buntic. Furthermore, the following civilians," and then come actually those listed in the annex that we talked about. Witness, how was it possible to distinguish who was a soldier and who was a civilian? Who made this distinction? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Civilians are civilians, and soldiers are those who are wearing a uniform with a weapon in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So do you know who lists those people, who --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in that same newspaper, on -- two pages further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: For Your Honours, for your orientation, page 9, there is actually an article saying, "Dubrovnik fire department in the war, by saving others, they jeopardised themselves."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And is that the incident where the fire workers were killed through a grenade while trying to save people from the Hotel Libertas? Is that what you referred to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had that in mind. And these are the three names that I mentioned a moment ago, Mihocevic, Savinovic, and Paskojevic. And the other two who went to help them and who, unfortunately, got killed, their names are also missing. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, at that time, when the -- when Dubrovnik was shelled and in particular, the old town was shelled, were you in any position or in any military command position, or what did you at that time and what were you, in particular in the time period in mid-November 1991 and 6th December?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I was in Dubrovnik. I wasn't at any military position. I was the mayor of Dubrovnik. If you meant exactly in which house, then sometimes in the municipality building, sometimes in the St. Ivan fortress, because we felt it was safer there. Also, we had no electricity or water or anything else, so the only electricity supply to have a telephone, because there were no mobile telephones as today, we used a generator that was put in a well-concealed spot so that it wouldn't be shelled so that we were able to have a telephone line and communication with the world. And for a while, it was the only one we had. We spent some time not only at the foot of the St. Ivan fortress but also up at the top, in the studio of a well-known Dubrovnik artist, Djuro Politika.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this St. Ivan fortress and the municipal building, are they in the old town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the old town, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And according to your observations and your knowledge, were there any military installations in the old town in the time period from October to the 6th of -- October to the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I really and sincerely am not aware of any military installations in the old town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were there any artillery positions in the old town or immediately in the vicinity of the old town? Do you know? And I'm only referring to this time period, October to 6 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I do not know of any artillery position in the old town. I never heard that any kind of shell was fired from the old town, and I was there. As far as I know, the closest position to the town was a mortar of a small range in the Gradac park, which was relatively close to the old town. And probably -- I'm no military expert but I believe that was so because the range of the weapon was such that it could reach Zarkovica. I'm only assuming that; I can't assert that with certainty. Talking about that, there was an anti-aircraft gun. I think it was a 20-millimetre gun which we somehow managed to get hold of, without a cap or a cap that wasn't functioning. And then we repaired it. And that gun was moved around on a small truck from one position to another so as to give the impression that we had several such weapons. And I repeat, it was a 20-millimetre gun. May military experts correct me, it may be 22 millimetres. Anyway, somewhere around 20 millimetres, and it did approach the town, come close, because the road is along the walls. So it may have passed by. And I know that at one point, it was near the Dubravka restaurant on this truck. Whether it was there for five minutes or five hours, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Gradac park, how far away is it from the old town, in metres?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately 500 metres as the crow flies, let's say, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that this moving 20- or 22-millimetre gun may have been on the road. Did it ever shoot when it was in the vicinity of the old town? Do you know that? In particular, in this time period in mid-November 1991 and December 1991, 6th December.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I guarantee that it did not. I guarantee no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those -- the gun that you mentioned, or other military objects, were they ever close to the hotels where the refugees were housed in Babin Kuk or this Libertas Hotel? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that they were. And as I knew people from the headquarters, I don't think that they would have allowed themselves to do anything of the sort. Precisely because they were aware of the danger of having those unfortunate people in the hotel suffer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were any soldiers stationed, or any units of soldiers, or the police stationed in the old town during this period October to 6th December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: Many young men who were in the Croatian army were from the old town. And many of them, when they would get one, two, or three days off, I'm speaking off the top of my head, let's say eight days, after spending eight days in their positions, they would go home. They would come into town. And quite certainly, you could see a soldier, one or two soldiers, in uniform entering the town. But that they were stationed in any of the buildings in town, I really don't know that there were any such cases, and I am almost ready to swear that there were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These soldiers that you mentioned, where were they actually stationed? Where were they -- where was the front line?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: 200 metres from the Argentina Hotel. That was the last outpost, the last position or the first position depending on which way you look at it, the Montenegrin army. Right above the Argentina Hotel that's where they had their - what shall I call it? - bunker or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put again to the witness the map of Exhibit 326, tab 13, the map of the Dubrovnik town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate that on this map, or is it not on the map at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No. It's hidden. It's to the right of the town here. I'd need to have the page unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: What I'm indicating here is the Argentina Hotel. And they were right up here on the hill, which is about 200 metres, give or take 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how far is it from the old town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. About 500, 600, or 700 metres perhaps, thereabouts. Seven or eight hundred metres, let's say. We can calculate it actually. This is 300. 650 to 700 metres as the crow flies, in direct line.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where was the military headquarters at that time where Mr. Marinovic was? Can you show that, where Mr. Marinovic was with his staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Up here where I am indicating, the area is called Lapad. It is an area called Lapad. There is a hotel there called the Zagreb Hotel, and another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were any soldiers or military units stationed in or close to the refugees hotels that you mentioned that were shelled?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Near Babin Kuk, no. But around this hotel in which the headquarters were located, I'm sure there were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that would be, as you said, Lapad. And can you say which hotels? Can you say in which hotels the soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Sumatrin and Zagreb. Those were the names of the hotel. Was it called Zagreb? Yes, I think it was the Zagreb Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. These shellings that you say that were particularly intense on the 10th, 11th, and 12th November and on the 6th of December, were they provoked by the people or the army -- the defenders of Dubrovnik? Do you know anything to this effect?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: We were not in a position to provoke. With respect to the attackers, we were completely powerless. They were the third or fourth strongest army in Europe, and we numbered less than 100 men to begin with. So there can be no question of any kind of provocation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that you didn't have electricity. What about water? Can you say something about the provision of water from the 1st of October to the 6th of December? Can you say anything to that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: There was a piece of information about that. Up until the summer, we didn't have electricity for 153 days. And I think for 132 days, there was no water, although there was a reserve -- how shall we call it -- backup possibility whereby we received small quantities of water from bypassing waterway from an old pipeline, water pipeline, that dated back to the French. The experts will know all about that. But that particular water line, supply line, gave very small quantities of water from time to time. And when I say at least a small amount of water, this would be a few-odd liters. But they were very valuable to us because the town was in a dreadful, catastrophic state, epidemics threatened to hit the town, and there were more people in the town than ever before in its history. So had the rain not fallen in November, everything would have ended much tragically than it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say a few-odd liters, does that mean a few-odd liters per person a day, or what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: There were times when I personally, who was the number one man in the municipality, I would have 1 litre of water per day for all my requirements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you are referring to the time period 1st October -- starting on the 1st October?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Couldn't you get water from the sea?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, they were just 2 or 300 metres away from us, and they had their snipers cock at us. And no one was able to put their noses outside the walls. And very often we were targeted within the ramparts, within the town walls where we were moving around, they could target us with their snipers, and did so. So nobody dared go out to fetch any water because there was a great likelihood that they would be killed if they were to do so, so that not even the water of the sea, sea water, could be used for the lavatory, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to move to the negotiations and the ultimatum that you already mentioned. And I would like to know from you whether you took part in a meeting on the 11th of October, 1991, with Admiral Jokic. And was that the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who attended from your side and from the army side, from the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: On the Croatian side, there was Mr. Zeljko Sikic who at the time was the president of the municipal government. Then there was Mr. Hrvoje Macun, who was in charge of communal affairs. There was Mr. Miso Mihocevic, who was an interpreter. There was myself. And just let me think back whether there was anybody else on our side. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And from the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: And on the JNA side, there was Admiral Jokic. There was, I think, a Lieutenant-Colonel was his rank, Dr. Svicevic, and Sofronije Jeremic, an Admiral. He later became an Admiral. I think he was captain of a military vessel at that time, but he advanced fairly rapidly and became Admiral later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Admiral Jokic indicate to you what his position was, what exact military position he had?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: We discussed the situation. On the ground, he was a new man for me. I had never seen him before. And at one point, he said that he was the one who commanded the units in the area which were moving towards the west, towards Dubrovnik and the town. Let me also mention, this was on the 11th, and Cavtat was still free, relatively free. Because up until Cavtat, everything else was occupied, Cavtat was still free.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Jeremic, what position did he have?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: I think he was an intelligence officer. I assume he was, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that? I mean, what is the basis of --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by everything; the negotiations, he was constantly negotiating, and I assumed that that was what his job was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Dr. Svicevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard, he was a doctor of wartime psychology. And I think that he was one of the organisers of the atmosphere and mood that was created with respect to our attacking them, which never, ever happened. And creating this atmosphere and mood on the other side with respect to the attack that Baca was threatened by with 30.000 armed Ustashas who had allegedly -- were on the move to take it over, take control of it. He was very arrogant in all the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who spoke -- did anyone on this occasion speak about the 30.000 armed Ustasha that was threatening Baca?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Not on that occasion, but before that, yes. And that's how they managed to recruit many people from Montenegro to go and march towards Dubrovnik, but not on that occasion; Konavle had already been taken over.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you had this meeting with Admiral Jokic and the other two, did they give a reason why they were attacking Dubrovnik? What did they say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: They persisted in claiming that there were 3, 1.000 or 7.000 terrorists, mercenaries, Kurds - those figures differed - and God knows who else, and that they ought to surrender

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was that true? Did you have mercenaries --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. Not a single mercenary did we have in our army at all. There was one foreigner. Yes, go ahead, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: There was one foreigner in our army, and that was a Dutchman who was married to a woman from Dubrovnik and who happened to find himself in Dubrovnik when the attack was launched. And he volunteered as a volunteer in the Croatian army. And as luck would have it, he's still alive and I hope he's living in the Netherlands. He was a very decent man. I don't know what his name was but I would recognise him if I saw him today.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you tell this to Admiral Jokic? Did you tell him that's wrong and --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did he react to that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Nothing. He didn't react at all. He just went on just as if I had not said anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you complain about what was happening to the town and to the region?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC
utterances.text: There was no reaction. They just continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned an ultimatum given to you. And with the help of the usher, I would like to put to you Exhibit 361, tab 39. And actually, the translation -- do we have the translation? The translation is actually in a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to adjourn, in fact, today prompt, at quarter to. So I think we'll adjourn now since it has come to the time. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you're not going to be very much longer, I trust, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it's actually something like 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. No more, please, because we must finish the examination-in-chief and also have time for cross-examination and to deal with any administrative matters which we need to next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to tell you something, and it's also for the witness and the other participants here. I will not be available on the 18th, so my colleague Mr. Nice will continue the examination and also be present during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The newspaper article spoken of by Ms. Laber is now available. I've got what looks like her original. I haven't spoken to her about it yet. It may be that the Chamber will be happy to accept simply copies. They come on rather large-size paper because it's the only way of fitting it in, but if I can make those available. The document that I had forecast being available today dealing with timetable issues is available. It is being filed today. But I will provide what are called courtesy copies to everyone, including the accused, I hope, before he leaves, so that people can have time to consider that between now and next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have the number of the article again. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 360.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. On the document coming your way by way of courtesy copy dealing with timetable matters, there's one attachment, attachment B, that is in a first form, it needs to be amplified, and I'm hoping to have it properly amplified by next Wednesday, but certainly in a more advanced stage than it is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Poljanic, I'm afraid we are not sitting, the Trial Chamber in this trial - we have other matters to attend to - before next Wednesday. So could you be back, please, next Wednesday when we shall return to this trial when we will finish your evidence. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.47 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday the 18th day of December, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
